concepts.title: Components
concepts.why: Components are reusable building blocks — like LEGO bricks you snap together to build a UI.

explain.eli5: A component is a function that returns some UI. Call it once, get one brick. Call it ten times, get ten identical bricks you can arrange however you like.
explain.standard: A React component is a function returning JSX. Name it in PascalCase. Rendering <Hello /> calls the function and inserts its output into the tree.
explain.deep: Components are pure functions of their inputs (props). React calls them to produce a virtual tree, diffs it against the previous one, and applies minimal DOM updates. Keep them pure and side-effect-free during render.

concepts.predict: If you render <Hello /> three times, how many <h1> elements appear? (Answer: three.)

challenge.prompt: Create a <Badge /> component that renders the text 'New'. Then render it twice.
check: App renders Badge at least twice

misconceptions: Forgetting PascalCase (react treats lowercase as HTML tags).
Returning multiple siblings without a wrapper or <>...</> fragment.

concepts.title: Props
concepts.why: Props let ONE component render MANY different outputs — the key to reuse.

explain.eli5: Props are the inputs you pass to a component, like arguments to a function. Same brick, different label.
explain.standard: Pass data via attributes: <KpiCard label="Open" value="9" />. Read them from the props object (often destructured) inside the component.
explain.deep: Props are read-only (immutable from the child's view). This one-way data flow makes rendering predictable. Type them with an interface in TS so the compiler enforces the contract.

concepts.predict: What renders for <Badge text="Beta" />? (Answer: a span containing 'Beta'.)

challenge.prompt: Turn KpiCard into a prop-driven component that accepts label, value, and icon, then render two different KPIs.

misconceptions: Trying to reassign props inside the child.
Forgetting the curly braces to embed a JS value in JSX.

concepts.title: Children & Composition
concepts.why: The `children` prop lets you write ONE generic container (like Card) and reuse it everywhere.

explain.eli5: children is whatever you put between the opening and closing tags. Card wraps it in a nice box without caring what's inside.
explain.standard:
Accept `children: ReactNode` and render {children}. Now and
    …
 share the same styling.
explain.deep: Composition beats configuration: instead of a Card with 20 boolean props, pass content as children. This is React's answer to inheritance — compose, don't extend.

concepts.predict: Can one Card wrap a KpiCard and another Card wrap a whole task list? (Answer: yes — that's the point.)

challenge.prompt: Write a Card that renders its children, then wrap two totally different pieces of UI with it.

misconceptions: Forgetting to actually render {children}.
Over-configuring with props instead of composing.

concepts.title: Lists & Keys
concepts.why: Render many components from data with .map — add DATA, not markup.

explain.eli5: Have a list of things? .map turns each item into a component. Give each a unique key so React can tell them apart.
explain.standard: kpis.map(k => <KpiCard key={k.id} {...k} />). The key must be stable and unique among siblings.
explain.deep: Keys let React's reconciler match old and new list items, preserving state and minimizing DOM churn. Never use array index as key for reorderable/removable lists.

concepts.predict: Add a 3rd object to KPIS — how many cards render now? (Answer: three, with no markup changes.)

challenge.prompt: Given an array of 3 tasks, render a <TaskItem> for each with a proper key.
challenge.starter:
const tasks = [ {id:1,text:'A'}, {id:2,text:'B'}, {id:3,text:'C'} ];
// map tasks -> <TaskItem key=... text=... />

misconceptions: Using the array index as key.
Forgetting the key entirely (console warning).

concepts.title: State with useState
concepts.why: State is memory that survives re-renders and drives what the UI shows.

explain.eli5: useState gives your component a variable it remembers, plus a button to change it. Change it → the UI updates automatically.
explain.standard: const [count, setCount] = useState(0). Call setCount(next) to update; React re-renders with the new value. Never mutate state directly.
explain.deep: State updates are asynchronous and batched. Use the updater form setCount(c => c + 1) when the next value depends on the previous. Each useState call is tied to render order — never call hooks conditionally.

concepts.predict: Click the button 3 times — what does it show? (Answer: Count: 3.)

challenge.prompt: Build a Counter with + and − buttons that never goes below 0.

misconceptions: Mutating state (count++) instead of calling the setter.
Calling hooks inside conditions or loops.

concepts.title: Events & Controlled Inputs
concepts.why: Controlled inputs keep the UI and your state perfectly in sync.

explain.eli5: Tie an input's value to state. When the user types, you update state; the input shows exactly what's in state.
explain.standard: value={draft} + onChange={e => setDraft(e.target.value)} makes a controlled input. Handle Enter with onKeyDown.
explain.deep: Controlled components make the React state the single source of truth, enabling validation, formatting, and conditional disabling. Uncontrolled inputs (refs) are an escape hatch for perf or integrating non-React code.

concepts.example:
const [draft, setDraft] = useState('');
<input value={draft} onChange={e => setDraft(e.target.value)} />
concepts.predict: If state is 'hi' and you type 'x', what does the input show? (Answer: 'hix'.)

challenge.prompt: Make a text input that shows a live character count below it.
challenge.starter:
const [text, setText] = useState(''); // controlled input +

{text.length} chars

misconceptions: Setting value without onChange (input becomes read-only).
Reading e.target.value after an await without capturing it first.

concepts.title: State Down, Events Up (Lifting)
concepts.why: When two components need the same data, move state to their shared parent and pass callbacks down.

explain.eli5: The parent holds the list. It hands data DOWN as props and hands children a phone number (callback) to call UP when something happens.
explain.standard: Parent owns tasks + add/toggle/remove. Children (AddTaskForm, TaskItem) receive onAdd/onToggle via props and invoke them — they never own the list.
explain.deep: Lifting state creates a single source of truth and one-way data flow. If prop-drilling gets deep, reach for Context or a store — but only when the pain is real.

concepts.predict: Who owns the task array — the form or the board? (Answer: the board, the parent.)

challenge.prompt: AddTaskForm has local input state but calls onAdd(text) to hand the value to TaskBoard. Wire it up.

misconceptions: Duplicating the list in both parent and child.
Mutating the array instead of returning a new one.

concepts.title: Data-Driven UI
concepts.why: Keep data in its own file so components stay dumb and swappable — replace mock data with an API and the UI won't change.

explain.eli5: Numbers live in a data file. The Dashboard just draws whatever the data says. Change data → UI follows.
explain.standard: Export KPIS from data/kpis.ts; Dashboard imports and maps it. No hard-coded numbers in components.
explain.deep: Separating data from presentation isolates change. The same components render mock data today and fetched data tomorrow; tests can inject fixtures; designers can tweak UI without touching business data.

concepts.predict: To add a metric, do you edit the Dashboard or the data file? (Answer: just the data file.)

challenge.prompt: Move a hard-coded KPI array out of the component into data/kpis.ts and import it.
challenge.starter:
// BEFORE: array is inline in Dashboard
// TODO: export it from data/kpis.ts and import
check: Data exported from its own module

misconceptions: Leaving business data hard-coded in JSX.
Mixing fetch logic into presentational components.

concepts.title: Derived & Conditional Rendering
concepts.why: Compute values from state at render time instead of storing them — fewer bugs, one source of truth.

explain.eli5: Don't store 'remaining count' in state — just count the unfinished tasks each render. Show an empty message only when the list is empty.
explain.deep: Derived state avoids sync bugs where two pieces of state disagree. Memoize expensive derivations with useMemo only after profiling shows a need.

concepts.example:
const remaining = tasks.filter(t => !t.done).length; return tasks.length === 0 ?

All clear ✨

: ;
concepts.predict: Should 'remaining' be its own useState? (Answer: no — derive it from tasks.)

challenge.prompt: Show '{remaining} of {total} remaining' and an empty state, both derived from the tasks array.
challenge.starter: // derive remaining + total from tasks; conditionally render empty state
challenge.solution:
const total = tasks.length, remaining = tasks.filter(t=>!t.done).length; return total === 0 ?

Empty

: <>

{remaining} of {total} remaining

;

misconceptions: Storing derived values in state and forgetting to update them.
Using && with a number (0 && <X/> renders 0).

concepts.title: Side Effects with useEffect
concepts.why: useEffect runs code AFTER render for things outside React — timers, subscriptions, syncing to storage.

explain.eli5: Sometimes you need to do something after the screen updates, like save to disk. useEffect is where that goes.
explain.standard: useEffect(() => { /* effect */ return () => {/* cleanup */}; }, [deps]). It runs when deps change.
explain.deep: Effects synchronize your component with external systems. The dependency array controls re-runs; the cleanup prevents leaks. Prefer deriving during render over effects; reach for effects only for true side effects.

concepts.predict: If remaining doesn't change, does the effect re-run on other renders? (Answer: no.)

challenge.prompt: Update document.title to the number of open tasks whenever it changes.
challenge.starter: // useEffect that sets document.title from `remaining`, dep [remaining]

misconceptions: Missing dependencies (stale values).
Forgetting cleanup for subscriptions/timers.
Using an effect for something derivable during render.

concepts.title: Persistence with localStorage
concepts.why: Make tasks survive a refresh — still 100% frontend, no database.

explain.eli5: Save the list to the browser's little notebook (localStorage) whenever it changes, and read it back on startup.
explain.standard: Load initial state from localStorage in useState's initializer; write to it in a useEffect keyed on the data.
explain.deep: localStorage is synchronous and string-only — JSON.stringify/parse around it. For larger/async needs use IndexedDB. Guard for SSR where window is undefined.

concepts.example:
const [tasks, setTasks] = useState(() => JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('tasks') || '[]'));
useEffect(() => { localStorage.setItem('tasks', JSON.stringify(tasks)); }, [tasks]);
concepts.predict: After adding a task and refreshing, is it still there? (Answer: yes.)

challenge.prompt: Persist the task list to localStorage and restore it on load.
challenge.starter: // lazy initializer reads localStorage; effect writes on change

misconceptions: Storing objects without JSON.stringify.
Reading localStorage on every render instead of a lazy initializer.

concepts.title: Custom Hooks
concepts.why: Extract reusable stateful logic into a function starting with 'use' — the ultimate reuse.

explain.eli5: A custom hook is your own mini-tool made of other hooks. Package the task logic once, use it in any component.
explain.standard: function useTasks(initial){ const [tasks,setTasks]=useState(initial); const add=…; return { tasks, add, toggle, remove }; }
explain.deep: Custom hooks share logic, not state — each call gets its own state. They compose other hooks, enabling testable, reusable behavior (useLocalStorage, useToggle). Follow the rules of hooks.

concepts.predict: Do two components calling useToggle() share the same on/off value? (Answer: no — separate state each.)

challenge.prompt: Write useTasks() that encapsulates the tasks array plus add/toggle/remove, then use it in TaskBoard.

misconceptions: Naming it without the 'use' prefix.
Expecting shared state across calls.
Calling it conditionally.
